# The Tax Wedge in the Reform Estimates {#sec-app-fiscal-wedge}

A tax change can move reported materials shares mechanically, without any change in overreporting: prices and the tax paid on sales and purchases adjust to the new rates. In addition, a a missing tax-wedge in estimation could generate a omitted-variable bias. The two-tax model isolates the part of this adjustment that runs through the sales-tax rates. With different rates on sales, $\tau_S$, and on purchases, $\tau_P$, the gross materials share carries the wedge $\ln\big((1-\tau_S)/(1-\tau_P)\big)$, which depends on the rates themselves. The 1983 reform changed those rates in the liable industries. After the reform, a rise in the gross share could reflect either more overreporting or this wedge. The event study in @sec-fiscal uses the share net of sales taxes, which removes the wedge.

@tbl-fiscal-wedge estimates the wedge's contribution directly, the same event study, with the gross minus the net share as the outcome. Its coefficients equal the gap between the event study on the gross share and on the net share. In liable industries, the wedge does not move before the reform. After it, the wedge rises by between 0.003 and 0.010 for unincorporated firms in liable industries, between a twentieth and a fifth of their response measured on the gross share. For proprietorships in 1984--1986, it rises by 0.011 to 0.013, between two fifths and all of their response in those years. A diff-in-diff study on the gross share would attribute this mechanical component to overreporting.

## Aggregate estimates of sales-tax evasion {#sec-app-vat-evasion}

@fig-app-vat-evasion reproduces an estimate of the sales tax on domestic transactions collected as a percentage of its potential revenue, computed from Colombia's national accounts [@Sanchez1994, p. 107]. The authors title the series "evasion of the domestic sales tax" (*evasión del IVA interno*); the uncollected share is 100 minus the plotted value. The series starts in 1984, the year the reform took effect. The uncollected share rose from 58 percent in 1984 to between 68 and 71 percent in 1987--1990 and fell to 65 percent in 1991. Overreporting by unincorporated firms follows the same path (@fig-fiscal-all).

![Sales tax on domestic transactions collected as a percentage of its potential revenue, Colombia, 1984--1991. The uncollected share, 100 minus the plotted value, measures evasion. Source: @Sanchez1994 [Gráfico 4, p. 107], computed from the national accounts.](/figures/appG-vat-evasion-sanchez1994.png){#fig-app-vat-evasion width=75%}
